recovery_horizon_sensitivity.note: The modelled reconstitution horizon is an ASSUMPTION, not an observation: no source says a struck refinery is substantially restored after this many days. Almost the whole headline decays on it, because observed and estimated recovery evidence covers only a handful of facilities. Halving and doubling the horizons moves the headline between 1.6 and 13.64 against a declared 5.68. Published as a sensitivity, not a tuning knob — the declared horizons are unchanged, and the way to narrow this range is recovery evidence, not a better guess.

cannot_tell_you.question: How much gas or coal infrastructure is disrupted
cannot_tell_you.answer: Not known. Gas and Coal have no published capacity denominator, so they are excluded from the composite and their weight redistributed. Recorded events in these sectors, none of them scored: Gas 8, Coal 0. A sector with no recorded event is not measured either, so that is not evidence that none occurred. Excluded is not zero.

cannot_tell_you.question: How much capacity a given strike actually removed
cannot_tell_you.answer: Not known for 173 of the 173 events where the question has a unit in this model. Open reporting almost never states it, and nothing here fills that gap with an estimate. A further 11 event(s) struck facilities carrying no modelled capacity magnitude, where the question has no unit rather than an unknown answer. Of the applicable events, 46 hit a facility whose own capacity is itself unrecorded. The index measures capacity AT disrupted sites — exposure, not loss.

cannot_tell_you.question: Every strike that has occurred
cannot_tell_you.answer: No. 116 oil-sector strikes dated within the benchmark's period (to 2026-06-30) are enumerated against a reported benchmark of 305 (38%). The remainder are counted in aggregate by the source without individual dates, so they cannot become events here. Other sectors have no benchmark at all.

cannot_tell_you.question: What fraction of the grid is offline
cannot_tell_you.answer: Not known, and this figure is not it. Transmission is scored as a weighted count of concurrent facility-events against a chosen saturation constant, not against any measure of grid capacity. The published sweep moves it roughly fourfold across plausible constants.

cannot_tell_you.question: What share of export terminal throughput is affected
cannot_tell_you.answer: Not known. Oil logistics has no published throughput denominator and borrows the refining capacity base as a proxy, so its value is a share of refining capacity — not of terminal throughput.

cannot_tell_you.question: The true current installed generating base
cannot_tell_you.answer: Not known. The census vintage is 2018 (newest Russian commissioning year; no retirement field), and it over-counts post-2018 retirements, under-counts post-2018 additions. The measured effect on the index is published with the project's methodology documentation.

cannot_tell_you.question: Whether a specific facility has actually been repaired
cannot_tell_you.answer: Usually not. 49 struck facilities are still counted in the index with no report that closes the disruption (6 of them carry a partial-restart or restoration report that did not close it), so their decline over time is modelled decay, not evidence of repair. Where a restoration WAS observed, the record says so and the evidence kind travels with the number.

cannot_tell_you.question: Where units are, what is combat-ready, or what should be struck next
cannot_tell_you.answer: Out of scope by design and permanently so. This models publicly reported disruption to energy infrastructure aggregated to administrative region. It holds no unit positions, no readiness or fuel state, no vulnerability assessment of undamaged assets, and no targeting value of any kind. Events carry no coordinates.

theatre.build_date_note: The build date says when this page was generated. It says nothing about how old any source is. Each source below carries its own release, retrieval and content dates.

impacts.scope_statement: Reviewed, publicly reported disruptions to energy systems and essential civilian services, from 2022 to the present. An attack or sabotage record is published for the country only, in every country; any other record at country or first-level-region precision, never finer. Each record says what service was affected, what kind of cause is reported, who is publicly said to be responsible and how firmly, and how strong the public evidence is.
caveats: This is not a census. Disclosure laws differ, operators may not disclose, conflicts distort reporting and media ecosystems differ from country to country.
A count here is a number of published records in this corpus. It is never a rate, and counts are never compared or ranked across countries.
Nothing here is scored. No record enters any index, any country system's event count or any research assessment.
A country that appears only here is not a monitored system: no index, no research-maturity claim, and no implied complete record for that country.
An attack or sabotage record is published for the country only, with no place, operator, method, headline or later status.

Evidence confidence describes the sources a record cites, not everything published about the event. It is not a probability, not severity and not a statement about how important any infrastructure is.

limitations: The corpus is a sample, not a census: each research pass searched one region or theme within a search budget, and an incident not found here is not evidence that none happened.
Many international wire services and several national outlets refused automated requests, so wire-level corroboration is often second-hand; each source family states where.
Official archives were enumerated in a few places only, as each source family states; elsewhere an official statement is usually read as carried by a news outlet.

Some widely reported disruptions are not in this corpus. Weather-driven power outages in the United States (Hurricanes Ian, Beryl, Helene and Milton, and Winter Storm Elliott) are recorded in the United States country system and are not filed again here. Other examples: any record for India or China; the December 2023 cyberattack on fuel-station payments in Iran; utility losses in the February 2023 earthquakes in Türkiye and Syria and the January 2024 Noto earthquake in Japan. Most were not reached within the search budget. Their absence here says nothing about whether or how they happened.

Coverage of kinetic attacks and sabotage is thin: few such records are published, only a handful for Ukraine's power system since 2022, and none from the 2026 Gulf conflict, whose attack records, where published, are on the country systems' own pages. The corpus is not a record of attacks.
Outages of single generating assets appear only where a research pass happened to find them; no systematic source for them was searched, so those records are a sample, not a list.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Ransomware
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Systems were encrypted or locked and a ransom demanded.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Denial of service
cyber_mechanisms.definition: A service was flooded with traffic until it could not respond.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Unauthorised access
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Someone without permission entered systems; no further mechanism is reported.

cyber_mechanisms.label: IT outage affecting operations
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Business computer systems went down and operations stopped or slowed as a result.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Operational technology disruption
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Systems that control physical equipment were disrupted.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Supply chain compromise
cyber_mechanisms.definition: The disruption came through software or equipment from a supplier.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Malicious configuration change
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Settings were deliberately changed so that a service failed.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Destructive malware
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Malicious software built to damage systems or stop them working.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Service provider compromise
cyber_mechanisms.definition: The disruption came through an outside company that runs systems for the operator.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Cyber-physical disruption
cyber_mechanisms.definition: A cyber incident reported to have caused a physical effect.

cyber_mechanisms.label: Mechanism not reported
cyber_mechanisms.definition: Sources call the incident cyber and do not say what kind.

absence_words.label: Unknown
absence_words.definition: Researched; public sources do not say.

absence_words.label: Withheld
absence_words.definition: Known and deliberately not published under the scope rules.

absence_words.label: No public evidence
absence_words.definition: Researched; no public source was found.

absence_words.label: Source inaccessible
absence_words.definition: A source exists and could not be opened.

regional_context.statement: Dated, sourced statements about the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, in aggregate: shipping, trade, supply, markets, reserves, policy and broad civilian and environmental effects. Each statement is as of its own date.
regional_context.not_built: There is no open or closed flag and no current status: only what a named source said, and when. Nothing here identifies a ship, a port, a facility or a path, and nothing here enters an index, a count or a country's record. A market movement is never presented as infrastructure loss.

context_vintage.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, International Energy Statistics
context_vintage.update_cadence: annual, with a monthly oil series; refreshed by an analyst, never by the daily build
context_vintage.note: National energy statistics. Separate from how recently each country's incident record was researched.
